before.family_text:
The first manuscript page of this spread is largely unreadable. Surviving words refer to hills, wreaths of flowers, midnight, thoughts, and things that have gone.
The more readable second page reflects on time and death. Years pass; people live and love, experience joys and follies, and feel regret. Death breaks the bonds of life. The poem then turns to the writer’s own generation:
“Soon shall we pass away …
To tell that we have been a simple tale,
Like some frail gossamer, wafted by the wind,
We’ll go and none may ever mark the place
Where we may fall …”
It continues that the busy people who follow will have little time to pause when the present generation has gone. Young people will laugh on, but the last lines are not fully legible.

after.family_text:
The first manuscript page of this spread is largely unreadable. It mentions hills, wreaths of flowers, midnight, and thoughts of things that might have been.

The facing page is more readable. These scenes and thoughts awaken us, and we forget the Indigenous person’s grave and the white person’s tomb. They lived and loved, knew joys and follies, yet death broke the cherished bonds that held them to life. The draft then speaks of idle mourning over their revered remains and of desecrating tombs raised by affection to honor and guard the dead. Part of the revised wording remains unclear.

Soon we will pass away, leaving [[unreadable wording]] behind to tell what we were: a single trace. Like fragile spider silk carried by the wind, we will go, and no one may ever mark where we fall. This busy race will have no time to pause when we are gone. The young and cheerful will laugh on, led by life’s [[unreadable wording]]. The final revised line cannot be read securely.

A focused comparison with the clearer poem enabled correction of several words on manuscript page 31, followed by a fresh visual check of the draft. The earlier provisional opening “Years come, our forms resemble” was rejected; the visible line reads “These scenes these thoughts awake.” Remaining differences and gaps are retained.

The first page remains very faint. It includes “to dream,” “to gaze,” and fragments concerning love and changing scenes.

On the facing page, no answer comes from the speaker’s surroundings. Silence and gloom are constant companions. The speaker feels lonely, as though sunk to the sea’s deepest depths, where the [[uncoffined?]] dead lie decaying. The poem asks when this dreadful desolation will end, binding the soul in suffering. The last question and the line about a new morning remain incomplete.

A clearer related version is Bachelor’s Lament at 10-047, but its wording differs from this draft.
